full_story_part2.text: Before class, I mark the passages I want to discuss with my middle school Japanese class. Looking at the lesson plan spread across the teacher's desk, I think about where to add a check that everyone has put their phone away. I want them to focus on the text without worrying about their screens. But what I want to protect, beyond test scores, is not just a quiet classroom. It's time to hear, through words, how other people see things differently. I read over the parts I've marked, then suddenly stop. What if all the checks to see whether phones are put away leave less time to read the text that matters? It's my responsibility to keep the lesson moving. I can't think that a quiet classroom is enough.

attempts_log.asr_text: I review school budgets for the local government. I lay out the costs of managing devices and the papers on learning support on my desk and mark them with sticky notes. Is it right to count the cost of putting phones away as spending to help students do better in school? I start to write a note about the budget review, then stop. How can I explain the link between not using phones and being able to learn? The budget can't make money appear out of nowhere. I worry that spending money on the bags could mean cutting support for students who need help with learning. At the same time, I still can't tell whether this cost is necessary. Since I decide how the money is divided, I can't avoid explaining why.

full_story_part3_c2.text: After work, at the evening high school I attend, I take out my notebook and check whether I still have any work messages on my phone. I want to avoid using it during class. But can I really say with confidence, No matter what happens, I can stay away from work messages? I take both my work and my studies seriously. As an adult, I want to be responsible for both. In the margin of my notebook, I write what I want to tell the school. Before the bag is closed, I want the door to a conversation to stay open. I don't want to give away my responsibility for managing how I use my phone, too.

full_story_part3_c3.text: We all want to value the time we spend learning. But even when we want the same thing, what we stand to lose if a decision is wrong—and how much responsibility we must take on—are different. One bag can't hold everyone's idea of what counts as good. The power to decide how money is spent, the power to shape the classroom, and the responsibility to keep daily life going. Even when people have little say in decisions, the burdens they carry are no lighter. Even if what they need to protect matters deeply, they may not get to take part in the decision. Before we close the bag, are we shutting out even the acceptance someone has not yet found the words to express?
